text.p: Copper prices and aluminium rose on the London Metal Exchange on Tuesday, while in the U.S. gold received a boost from the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision not to raise interest rates.
Copper broke above the key $1,900 level as traders bought cash metal in response to the exchange's warehouses stocks falling more than forecast.
Most of the other base metals ticked higher in sympathy.
Three months copper firmed about $40 a tonne after stocks fell by 8,825 tonnes, nearly 6,000 tonnes more than expected.
Many analysts had been expecting copper to remain under pressure after slipping under $1,900 in late trading on Friday and losing ground again on Monday.
Aluminium edged up around $8.00 from Monday's depressed closing levels to about $1,400.
"I've seen some good consumer buying, but that doesn't mean it won't go lower," a floor trader said.
European grains prices were mostly lower led by wheat prices after rising in response to higher French prices last week.
Barley prices, especially in Britain, weakened on expectations that a recent 1.4 million tonne order from Saudi Arabia would be met largely from France.
U.S. soybean futures were lower also in response to improved growing conditions and the weakness spilled over to other grains futures in the Chicago and Kansas City markets.

CBOT wheat futures closed higher on follow-through technical buying plus firm cash basis markets, traders said. Traders said the market was due for a recovery after its recent slide with futures on Tuesday giving off signs of a seasonal recovery. Wheat closed 2-1/4 to 4-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with December up three at $4.29-1/2.

NYMEX gasoline prices ended Tuesday sharply higher, with crude and heating oil pushed up to a lesser extent, on a combination of bullish political news and refineries cutting operating rates. October gasoline ended 2.76 cents a gallon higher at 62.83 cents while October heating oil settled up 2.21 cents a gallon to 69.69 cents. November crude oil settled 70 cents higher at $24.07 a barrel. The October contract in crude expired last Friday. On the political front, doctors are set to decide Wednesday when they will operate on the heart of Russia's President Boris Yeltin. The market fears Yeltsin's ailing health could create political instability in the region. Russia is one of the world's largest oil producers. In the oil-rich Middle East, General Mohsen Rezaei, commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted in the daily Tehran Times as saying Tehran would strongly retaliate throughout the Gulf against any aggressive moves by the United States or Israel. Dealers said, however, that Tuesday's political news provided a bullish backdrop rather than any substantial fundamental support.
New York precious metals futures ended higher Tuesday, continuing this week's shortcovering rally, helped near the close by the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision not to raise interest rates.
COMEX gold ended up $1.30 an ounce at $385.70 an ounce, after trading in a $384.40-385.80 range on total gold futures estimated volume of 27,000 lots.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted $382.60/383.10, compared to the London afternoon fix at $382.30 and the New York close Monday at $381.50-382.00.
CSCE world sugar closed an active session barely above the day's lows, where steady trade buying managed to hold the market, floor sources said.

Fund selling in May emerged once the contract broke an uptrend line at 11.15, triggering selling in other months, one dealer said. Trade short-covering and producer buying held the March contract at an uptrend line.

While last week's flurry of liquidation reduced open interest in October, the speculative long position remains high. Open interest stood at 24,128, off 1,919 in October, while open interest in the March contract stood at 67,745, up 215 lots.
March settled off 0.23 to 11.04, having ranged from 11.30 to 11.02. Spot October closed 0.13 weaker at 11.17, while the back months eased 0.23 to 0.14 on the day.
